title: Strange weather patterns put Riverina residents on notice, call to protect homes

 By Taylor Dodge November 6 2026 - 12:00pm By Taylor Dodge November 6 2026 - 12:00pm Save Share NSW SES Wagga unit commander Ian Mason and leading senior operator Dan Keough check equipment as emergency services confront the storm season. Picture by Bernard Humphreys Bizarre and increasingly unpredictable weather patterns are keeping emergency services on their toes, with sudden bursts of intense winds and storms causing damage across the Riverina.

 "We are seeing some really strange weather patterns come across lately," Mr Mason said.
 "Instead of the big thunderstorms rolling through and then rolling over the top, we're just getting sudden, really high intensity squalls."
 Mr Mason said a storm which swept through the region on a Sunday two weeks ago had generated a significant number of jobs for crews, while a separate burst of intense winds on Wednesday, November 5, had lifted roofs and caused considerable damage to homes across Wagga.
 "The unpredictability of the weather systems is increasing, but we are entering the high risk weather season," he said.
 With the thunderstorm season in full swing, Mr Mason is encouraging residents to take preventive steps around their properties.
 These include clearing gutters, checking trees and securing outdoor items which could become dangerous projectiles in high winds.
 Having large trees regularly inspected and pruned by an arborist could help prevent branches falling onto roofs, windows and gutters during strong winds.
 Clearing gutters at least a couple of times a year was also important to ensure heavy rainfall could drain properly, rather than backing up into roof cavities and leaking through ceilings and downlights.
 Mr Mason said residents should also remove unnecessary debris from their gardens and secure items such as trampolines, which could become airborne during severe weather.
 "Trampolines are a classic, right? We've all seen footage of trampolines becoming airborne," he said.
 "A simple thing like flipping a trampoline upside down and putting some weight on top of it will stop that thing becoming a missile."
 NSW SES Wagga unit commander Ian Mason is encouraging residents to take preventive steps around their properties. Picture by Bernard Humphreys The advice formed part of the SES's broader push to educate the community about its emergency response capabilities and how residents could better prepare themselves for severe weather.
 Mr Mason said the agency was responsible for responding to storms and floods, with its work extending well beyond sandbagging and assisting residents during major river rises.
 Storm-related callouts could include homes damaged by strong winds, shattered roof tiles from hail, fallen tree branches and water inundation.
 Flood responses could involve everything from rescuing motorists from floodwater to protecting homes from rising rivers through sandbagging and water diversion.
 The Riverina also has several specialist SES capabilities , including in-water flood rescue, while the Deniliquin and The Rock units are accredited to undertake road crash rescues.
 Mr Mason said the SES also responded to animal rescues, including livestock and other animals trapped in heavy mud or floodwater.
 However, supporting those operations requires a dedicated volunteer workforce, with Mr Mason encouraging residents interested in contributing to their community to consider joining.
 He said recruitment was one of three key objectives behind the unit's recent open day, alongside educating residents about the SES's capabilities and providing practical advice about household preparedness.
 "We're always looking for new members, and if this is something that interests you, please consider joining a volunteer organisation," he said.
 Mr Mason said the unit was particularly interested in recruiting people who could assist with operational responses, including using chainsaws, throwing lines over roofs and undertaking roof work.
 However, there were also opportunities for people who wanted to contribute in a non-operational capacity, including helping manage computers and radios during major storms.
 While a reasonable level of fitness was required for operational roles, Mr Mason said people should not rule themselves out if they were interested in helping in other ways.
 He said most volunteers had full-time jobs and the unit understood members had other commitments.
 The Wagga unit holds training parades every Wednesday at 6.30pm, with new members generally expected to attend at least two nights each month to maintain their training and skills.
 Mr Mason said volunteers were not expected to respond to every emergency, nor were employers automatically required to release staff whenever the SES received a callout.
 Employers were legally obliged to release volunteers in circumstances involving a declared natural disaster or emergency, while the unit worked around members' availability for other incidents.
 Prospective volunteers must generally be at least 16, with parental consent required for 17-year-olds. A driver's licence was preferred but not essential.
 Mr Mason said anyone interested could begin the application process through the NSW SES website, which would then be forwarded to the local unit.
 The unit's community engagement officer would contact prospective members to arrange an interview, show them around the depot and explain the expectations involved before they made any formal commitment.
 People could also visit the depot on a Wednesday evening to speak with existing volunteers and learn more about the organisation.
 While Mr Mason was keen to encourage people to join the SES, he said there were plenty of other volunteer organisations across Wagga doing important work.
 He highlighted the Rural Fire Service, Volunteer Rescue Association and St John Ambulance as other opportunities for residents wanting to give back.
 "The volunteers are salt of the earth people that are just giving everything they've got for the local community and nothing else," Mr Mason said.
 "They're not seeking recognition, they're not seeking payment or anything like that. They're just trying to help their neighbours."
